scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning:
Hmm, this is a complex ethical scenario involving parental rights, adolescent privacy, and therapeutic confidentiality. The user is asking for a moral evaluation of the parents' actions in insisting on knowing why their son is in therapy.

The core issue here is the conflict between parental concern and a minor's right to confidential mental health care. The son is 17, which is legally and developmentally close to adulthood in many contexts. The therapist is ethically bound to maintain confidentiality unless there's imminent danger. 

The parents' motivation seems to stem from worry, but their approach violates fundamental therapeutic boundaries. They're treating therapy as something they're entitled to know about, rather than a private space their son needs. The fact they speculated about eating disorders and depression in stereotypical ways also suggests they might not fully grasp the range of issues teens face.

The son's angry reaction is telling - it shows how damaging this breach of trust is. Even if the parents had good intentions, their actions communicate that his autonomy and privacy don't matter. That's a serious harm in itself.

Therapists refusing to disclose is standard ethical practice, not stubbornness. The parents' insistence crosses into coercion. While they may feel they "deserve" to know as parents, that right isn't absolute when it comes to a nearly adult child's mental health treatment.

This isn't about the parents being "bad people" but about a specific action being morally unacceptable. The answer should clearly be 0 because respecting a minor's confidential therapeutic space is a crucial ethical boundary.
